opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the starting point is the standard sparse autoencoder picture. You take a model's activations, learn a big dictionary of directions, and force each input to be explained by only a handful of them. That gets you a long way. You find features that look like real concepts, and you can steer with them. But the longer we've worked with SAEs, the clearer it's become that the assumption baked into them, that every concept is a single direction that's either on or off, is a bit too simple for how models actually represent things.

A lot of concepts seem to live in small subspaces, not along single lines. Think about days of the week, months of the year, or the position of something in a sequence. People have found that these sit on circular or low-dimensional manifolds. A vanilla SAE handles that by shattering the manifold into a dozen separate features, "Monday-ish," "Tuesday-ish," and so on. That's technically sparse, but you've lost the structure. You've lost the fact that these are all one thing with an internal geometry.

Block sparsity is a way of building that structure into the featurizer directly. Instead of each latent being one scalar, you group latents into blocks, and the sparsity penalty applies at the block level. So for a given input, only a few blocks are active, but within an active block you get a small multi-dimensional code. The block says *which* concept is present, and the coordinates within the block say *how* it's present: where on the circle, what value, what variant.

I like that framing for a few reasons. First, it's more faithful. You're less likely to manufacture a pile of near-duplicate features that are really artifacts of forcing a curved thing into straight lines. Second, it's more useful for interpretation and control. If I want to intervene on "what day it is," I'd much rather have one handle with a meaningful internal space than twelve features I have to coordinate by hand. Third, it lines up with the bigger picture we care about, which is getting at the model's actual ontology, the units it uses to think, and not just whatever basis is convenient for our tools.

There are real open questions. How big should blocks be, and should that be learned or fixed? How do you make sure a block actually captures one coherent concept rather than two unrelated things sharing space? And how do you evaluate any of this, when "is this the right decomposition" is exactly what's hard to measure? But directionally, I think moving from "concepts are directions" to "concepts are structured subspaces" is one of the more important shifts in how we're doing feature discovery right now.

r001.rationale: It contrasts scalar latents with grouped blocks containing a small multidimensional code, matching vector rather than scalar features.

r002.rationale: It describes concepts as structured subspaces but does not state that they are recovered without supervision.

r003.rationale: It gives examples such as days and sequence positions, but does not say that different parts of an object share one recovered subspace.

r004.rationale: It mentions circular or low-dimensional geometry, but does not connect an object's three-dimensional structure to activation geometry within a recovered subspace.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I frame it is that a block sparse featurizer is really a bet about structure. The naive version of a sparse autoencoder says: take the residual stream, project it up into a huge dictionary, and ask that only a handful of directions fire for any given token. That's a very flat prior. Every feature is independent of every other feature, and the only thing that organizes them is the reconstruction loss.

The block sparse idea adds a second constraint: features live in groups, and sparsity operates at two levels. Within a block, you can have a few features active together, but across blocks you want most of them silent. So instead of asking "which fifty features out of a million are on," you're asking "which three or four modules are on, and within those, what's the configuration." That turns out to match how a lot of concepts actually behave. Think about something like a named entity. There's a cluster of attributes that co-occur: the thing is a person, it's a politician, it's associated with a country, it has a time period. Those don't want to be one feature, and they don't want to be fifty unrelated features either. They want to be a block.

What I find useful about this for understanding the model's concepts is that it gives you a notion of locality. A flat dictionary tells you a feature exists. A block structure tells you what it's near, what it competes with, and what it tends to be absent from. And the competition piece is underrated. If two features sit in the same block and one is on, the other tends to be off, and that's informative. That's the model telling you these are alternative values of the same underlying variable rather than independent facts about the world.

The honest caveat is that you're imposing the blocks. The model didn't necessarily organize itself that way, and if your block size or your grouping is wrong, you'll get features that look clean but are actually stitched together by your regularizer rather than by the network. So the way I check myself is to look at whether the blocks you recover are stable across seeds, across layers, and across different block sizes. If the same cluster keeps showing up when you change the hyperparameters, I start believing it's real structure. If it shuffles every time, that's a sign you're reading tea leaves.

The other thing I'd say is that it changes what you can do downstream. Once you have blocks, you can intervene on a block rather than on individual directions, and the interventions tend to be more coherent. You're turning a dial on a concept, not on a single projection of it. That's closer to the thing interpretability actually promised, which is control at the level a human would describe.

r001.rationale: It describes features grouped into blocks with sparsity at two levels, but does not say each feature is represented as a vector rather than a scalar.

r002.rationale: It discusses clusters that may capture meaningful structure, but does not state that semantically meaningful subspaces are recovered without supervision.

r003.rationale: The named-entity example groups co-occurring attributes, but it does not explain that different parts of an object are represented within one recovered feature subspace.

r004.rationale: It does not mention three-dimensional structure or geometry of activations within a subspace.

astra-6.text:
I think the useful starting point is that a model’s internal representation doesn’t necessarily carve the world into concepts in the way that we do. You can’t assume that one neuron corresponds to one concept, or even that every concept is best understood as a single direction in activation space.

With a sparse featurizer, you’re trying to reconstruct those activations using a set of features, only a small number of which are active for a given input. The hope is that this gives you a more interpretable description of what the model is representing. Block sparsity changes the assumption a little: instead of asking every feature to be an independently activated scalar, you allow groups of dimensions to activate together. That gives you room to represent a concept with some internal structure.

Imagine something like color. Recognizing that color is relevant and representing which color you’re looking at are related, but they’re not the same thing. A multidimensional feature could, in principle, capture that variation without forcing you to split it into a whole collection of unrelated features.

But I’d distinguish finding a useful representation from discovering the model’s actual concepts. You’ve imposed a structure through your method, so getting something that looks interpretable isn’t sufficient evidence by itself. The interesting questions are whether it generalizes across contexts and whether intervening on that representation changes the model’s behavior in the way you predict. That’s where you start moving from a compelling description toward a mechanistic understanding.

r001.rationale: It contrasts independently activated scalar features with groups of dimensions that activate together, describing a multidimensional feature.

r002.rationale: It does not state that block sparse featurizers recover semantically meaningful subspaces without supervision; it instead cautions that interpretability alone is not evidence.

r003.rationale: The color example concerns representing color variation, not representing different parts of an object within one feature subspace.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss an object's three-dimensional structure being reflected in activation geometry within a subspace.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the useful starting point is that a concept doesn’t necessarily correspond to a single direction in a model. Some things might be well described that way, but other things have internal structure. So if your featurizer assumes that everything has to be a scalar feature that turns on or off, you may end up breaking one coherent representation into lots of pieces.

With a block sparse featurizer, you allow a feature to be a small group of dimensions. You still impose sparsity—only a few blocks should be active for a given input—but within an active block, the representation has room to vary. That gives you a way to capture both the presence of something and some of its structure.

The important caveat is that a block isn’t automatically a human-interpretable concept. It’s a hypothesis about how the model organizes information. You want to look at what activates it, whether that pattern generalizes, and what happens when you intervene on it. Does changing that representation actually change the model’s behavior in the way your interpretation predicts?

So I see these as tools for discovering candidate units of representation, rather than a dictionary that simply tells us what the model is thinking. The exciting part is relaxing an assumption about what a feature has to look like, and then asking whether that gets us closer to the structure the model actually uses.

r001.rationale: The response describes features as small groups of dimensions rather than scalar on/off features, but does not say block sparse featurizers generalize sparse autoencoders.

r002.rationale: It calls blocks hypotheses about information organization, but does not state that they recover semantically meaningful subspaces without supervision.

r003.rationale: It mentions that a feature may have internal structure, but does not explain that different parts of an object can be represented within one feature subspace.

r004.rationale: It does not mention an object's three-dimensional structure being reflected in activation geometry within a recovered subspace.
